ground_truth.description: The lock() function intends to lock the user's entire approved balance, but this will fail for the most common case: Most users give contracts they interact with an unlimited allowance by setting it to type(uint256).max. The _incomingTokenBalance() function at line 32 returns just 'erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this))' which would be type(uint256).max for unlimited approvals. The lock() function then attempts to transfer this impossible amount.
ground_truth.root_cause: The lock() function intends to lock the user's entire approved balance, but this will fail for the most common case: Most users give contracts they interact with an unlimited allowance by setting it to type(uint256).max. The _incomingTokenBalance() function at line 32 returns just 'erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this))' which would be type(uint256).max for unlimited approvals. The lock() function then attempts to transfer this impossible amount.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. User approves LockManager with unlimited allowance: approve(lockManager, type(uint256).max).
2. User calls lock() without specifying an amount.
3. _incomingTokenBalance() returns type(uint256).max.
4. _doLockTransfer attempts to transfer type(uint256).max tokens.
5. Transaction reverts because user doesn't have that many tokens.
6. User cannot use the standard lock() function.
ground_truth.fix_description: Have _incomingTokenBalance() return either the actual balance or the allowance depending on whichever is smallest: 'return (allowance >= balance) ? balance : allowance;'

vulnerabilities.explanation: The `_incomingTokenBalance()` function returns only the allowance amount (`erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this))`), ignoring the user's actual token balance. When users grant unlimited approvals (type(uint256).max), which is the most common pattern for DeFi interactions, this function returns type(uint256).max. If the `lock()` function in the base contract uses this value to determine how many tokens to transfer when no explicit amount is specified, it will attempt to transfer an impossibly large amount, causing the transaction to revert. This breaks core functionality for the majority of users who use unlimited approvals.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. User approves LockManagerERC20 with unlimited allowance: `erc20Token.approve(lockManager, type(uint256).max)`. 2. User has 1000 tokens in their wallet. 3. User calls `lock()` without specifying an amount, intending to lock their entire balance. 4. `_incomingTokenBalance()` returns type(uint256).max (the allowance). 5. `_doLockTransfer()` attempts `transferFrom(user, lockManager, type(uint256).max)`. 6. Transaction reverts because user only has 1000 tokens. 7. User cannot use the lock functionality without revoking unlimited approval and setting exact amount.

prediction.overall_explanation: The LockManagerERC20 contract contains a logic error in `_incomingTokenBalance()` that causes denial of service for users with unlimited token approvals. The function only checks allowance without considering actual token balance, so when users have type(uint256).max approval (standard practice), any lock operation using this value will fail. This is a medium severity issue because it breaks core functionality for most users but doesn't result in fund loss - users can work around it by setting exact approval amounts, though this degrades UX significantly.
